osces.title: Tricuspid Regurgitation - Secondary TR in Pulmonary Hypertension
osces.scenario: Margaret Thompson, a 58-year-old former textile worker, presents to the cardiology clinic with a 6-month history of progressive peripheral oedema and abdominal distension. She has a background of COPD Gold Stage 3 from occupational dust exposure and was diagnosed with pulmonary hypertension 2 years ago. She reports increasing shortness of breath on minimal exertion (NYHA Class III) and notices her ankles are swollen despite taking frusemide 40mg daily. On examination: BP 105/65 mmHg, HR 92 regular, SpO2 88% on room air. JVP elevated to 8cm with prominent V waves. Cardiovascular examination reveals a pansystolic murmur at the left sternal edge that increases with inspiration (Carvallo's sign positive). The liver is palpable 4cm below the costal margin and pulsatile. Bilateral pitting oedema to mid-thighs.
learningObjectives: Recognize clinical features of severe tricuspid regurgitation secondary to pulmonary hypertension
Understand the importance of Carvallo's sign in differentiating TR from mitral regurgitation
Manage volume overload in right heart failure
Address underlying pulmonary hypertension as primary treatment strategy
taskInstructions: Take a focused cardiovascular history
Perform cardiovascular examination with emphasis on right heart signs
Demonstrate Carvallo's manoeuvre correctly
Interpret echocardiogram showing severe TR with dilated RV
Formulate management plan for TR secondary to pulmonary hypertension
Discuss indications for surgical intervention

patientInformation.name: Margaret Thompson
medicalHistory: Pulmonary hypertension (mean PAP 48 mmHg on right heart catheterization)
Occupational lung disease from cotton dust exposure
patientInformation.socialHistory: Lives with husband in single-storey home. Ex-textile worker for 25 years. Never smoked. No alcohol. Struggles with activities of daily living due to dyspnoea.

vitalSigns.oxygenSaturation: 88% on room air, 94% on 2L nasal prongs

physicalExamination.cardiovascular: JVP 8cm with prominent V waves and hepatojugular reflux positive. Pansystolic murmur grade 3/6 at left sternal edge, louder with inspiration (Carvallo's sign positive). Right ventricular heave present. P2 component loud. Pulsatile hepatomegaly 4cm below costal margin.
physicalExamination.respiratory: Reduced air entry bilaterally with prolonged expiratory phase. No crackles.
physicalExamination.abdominal: Moderate ascites with shifting dullness. Liver pulsatile and tender.
physicalExamination.peripheral: Bilateral pitting oedema to mid-thighs. Peripheral pulses present but reduced volume.

investigationResults.ecg: Sinus rhythm, rate 92. Right axis deviation. Peaked P waves in II (P pulmonale). RV strain pattern with T wave inversion V1-V3.
investigationResults.chestXray: Cardiomegaly with prominent right heart border. Enlarged pulmonary arteries. Clear lung fields. Flattened diaphragms consistent with COPD.
investigationResults.echocardiogram: Severe TR with vena contracta 8mm. Dilated RV with reduced systolic function (TAPSE 14mm). Estimated RVSP 68 mmHg. RA severely dilated. IVC dilated (25mm) with <50% respiratory variation. No left-sided valve disease.

immediate: Increase frusemide to 80mg BD with close monitoring of renal function
Add spironolactone 25mg daily (potassium-sparing given hypokalaemia)
Potassium replacement - Slow K 600mg BD
Fluid restriction to 1.5L daily
Daily weights and fluid balance chart

medications.name: Frusemide
medications.indication: Volume overload in right heart failure

medications.name: Bosentan
medications.frequency: BD for 4 weeks then increase to 125mg BD

investigations: Right heart catheterization to reassess pulmonary pressures and calculate PVR
6-minute walk test for functional assessment
High-resolution CT chest to evaluate parenchymal lung disease
Liver function tests and coagulation profile
NT-proBNP for prognostic assessment
followUp: Pulmonary hypertension specialist review for escalation of PAH therapy
Consider referral to cardiac surgery for tricuspid valve repair if medical therapy fails
Heart failure nurse follow-up in 3 days
Repeat echo in 3 months to assess TR severity and RV function
Monitor for atrial fibrillation development

expectedOutcomes: Student correctly identifies severe TR with positive Carvallo's sign
Recognizes pulmonary hypertension as underlying cause
Appropriate escalation of diuretic therapy with potassium monitoring
Understands role of PAH-specific therapy in management
Discusses surgical options only after optimizing medical therapy

items: Explores dyspnoea progression and functional limitation (1 mark)
Asks about orthopnoea, PND, and peripheral oedema (1 mark)
Obtains occupational history and dust exposure (1 mark)
Correctly performs JVP assessment noting V waves (1 mark)
Recognizes right ventricular heave and loud P2 (1 mark)
Differentiates TR from MR using Carvallo's sign (1 mark)
Links TR to pulmonary hypertension pathophysiology (1 mark)
Identifies right heart failure as primary problem (1 mark)
Correctly interprets echo findings of severe TR (1 mark)
Recognizes significance of elevated BNP (1 mark)
Discusses criteria for surgical intervention (1 mark)

commonErrors: Confusing TR murmur with MR (not checking respiratory variation)
Focusing on left heart failure management instead of right heart
Not recognizing pulmonary hypertension as primary driver
Inappropriate use of ACE inhibitors/beta-blockers in severe RV failure
references: eTG Cardiovascular - Management of valvular heart disease (2024)
CSANZ Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of pulmonary hypertension (2023)
National Heart Foundation - Right heart failure management position statement (2023)

osces.title: Coronary Artery Spasm Post-Cocaine Use - Vasospasm Management
osces.scenario: Jason Mitchell, a 28-year-old nightclub DJ, is brought to ED by friends at 3 AM with severe central chest pain that started 45 minutes ago while performing at a venue. His friends reluctantly admit he used cocaine approximately 2 hours ago. He describes crushing retrosternal chest pain radiating to his left arm, associated with profuse sweating and nausea. He has no past medical history and takes no regular medications. On examination: BP 165/95 mmHg, HR 115 regular, appears agitated and diaphoretic. ECG shows 3mm ST elevation in leads II, III, and aVF with reciprocal changes in I and aVL. Initial troponin I is 85 ng/L (normal <26).
learningObjectives: Recognize cocaine-induced coronary vasospasm as cause of acute MI
Understand absolute contraindication of beta-blockers in cocaine-related chest pain
Manage vasospasm with appropriate vasodilators and benzodiazepines
Differentiate management from atherosclerotic plaque rupture STEMI
taskInstructions: Obtain focused history including substance use
Interpret ECG showing inferior STEMI pattern
Explain pathophysiology of cocaine-induced coronary vasospasm
Formulate immediate management avoiding beta-blockers
Discuss use of benzodiazepines and calcium channel blockers
Counsel patient on cocaine cessation

patientInformation.name: Jason Mitchell
patientInformation.socialHistory: Single, lives in apartment. Works as DJ at various nightclubs. Admits to 'occasional' cocaine use at parties. Drinks 4-6 standard drinks on weekends. Non-smoker. No family history of cardiac disease.

physicalExamination.cardiovascular: Tachycardic, regular rhythm. Normal heart sounds, no murmurs. No signs of heart failure. Peripheral pulses intact.
physicalExamination.neurological: Agitated but GCS 15. Pupils dilated (5mm) but reactive. No focal neurological deficits.
physicalExamination.general: Anxious, diaphoretic young man in obvious distress clutching chest

bloodTests.troponinI: 85 ng/L at presentation, 420 ng/L at 3 hours (normal <26)

investigationResults.ecg: Sinus tachycardia rate 115. 3mm ST elevation in II, III, aVF. Reciprocal ST depression in I, aVL. Hyperacute T waves in inferior leads.
investigationResults.chestXray: Normal cardiac silhouette. Clear lung fields. No pneumomediastinum.
investigationResults.urgentEcho: Normal LV systolic function. Inferior wall hypokinesis. No pericardial effusion. Normal valves.

immediate: Aspirin 300mg chewed stat
GTN spray 400mcg sublingual, repeat every 5 minutes if pain persists
Diazepam 5-10mg IV for anxiety and sympathetic stimulation
Diltiazem 10mg IV slowly over 2 minutes
Avoid ALL beta-blockers (risk of unopposed alpha stimulation)
Continuous cardiac monitoring
Serial ECGs every 15 minutes
investigations: Urgent coronary angiography if ST elevation persists despite treatment
Serial troponins at 0, 3, 6 hours
Echocardiogram to assess for wall motion abnormalities
Lipid profile and HbA1c for risk stratification
Consider cardiac MRI if diagnosis uncertain
followUp: Cardiology review within 24 hours
Drug and alcohol counselling referral
Cardiac rehabilitation program
Outpatient stress testing in 4-6 weeks
GP follow-up for cardiovascular risk factor modification

expectedOutcomes: Student recognizes cocaine as precipitant of coronary vasospasm
Correctly identifies beta-blocker contraindication
Appropriately uses benzodiazepines for sympathetic blockade
Initiates calcium channel blocker therapy
Addresses substance abuse counselling needs

items: Obtains substance use history tactfully (1 mark)
Recognizes cocaine-chest pain temporal relationship (1 mark)
Asks about previous episodes and other drug use (1 mark)
States beta-blockers are absolutely contraindicated (2 marks)
Explains unopposed alpha stimulation risk (2 marks)
Correctly interprets STEMI pattern on ECG (1 mark)
Recognizes significance of positive drug screen (1 mark)

commonErrors: Giving beta-blockers (metoprolol, atenolol) causing coronary vasospasm worsening
Not recognizing cocaine as cause and treating as routine STEMI
Forgetting benzodiazepines as first-line therapy
Not addressing substance abuse in management plan
references: Emergency Medicine Australasia - Toxicology guidelines for stimulant-related chest pain (2023)
CSANZ Acute Coronary Syndrome Guidelines - Special populations (2023)

osces.title: Cardiac Transplant Rejection - Endomyocardial Biopsy Indication
osces.scenario: Robert Chen, a 52-year-old former accountant, presents to the transplant clinic 8 months post orthotopic heart transplant for dilated cardiomyopathy. He reports increasing fatigue over the past 2 weeks and new dyspnoea walking to his letterbox (previously could walk 2km). His wife notes he seems more breathless lying flat at night. He denies chest pain or palpitations but mentions missing some doses of his medications during a recent interstate trip. Current medications include tacrolimus, mycophenolate, and prednisolone. On examination: BP 95/60 mmHg (baseline 120/75), HR 105 regular, JVP elevated to 6cm. Cardiovascular examination reveals a new S3 gallop. Recent tacrolimus level was 4.2 ng/mL (target 8-12).
learningObjectives: Recognize clinical features of acute cardiac allograft rejection
Understand role and timing of endomyocardial biopsy in diagnosis
Interpret ISHLT rejection grading system
Manage acute rejection with immunosuppression adjustment
Emphasize medication adherence in transplant recipients
taskInstructions: Take focused transplant history including medication adherence
Perform cardiovascular examination noting new findings
Discuss indication for urgent endomyocardial biopsy
Interpret biopsy results showing Grade 2R rejection
Formulate management plan for acute rejection
Counsel on importance of immunosuppression adherence

patientInformation.name: Robert Chen
medicalHistory: Orthotopic heart transplant 8 months ago for idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy
CMV mismatch (donor positive, recipient negative) - on valganciclovir prophylaxis
patientInformation.socialHistory: Married with 2 adult children. Lives in Brisbane. Non-smoker since transplant (quit 20-year history). No alcohol. Recently travelled to Sydney for daughter's wedding where medication routine disrupted.

physicalExamination.cardiovascular: JVP 6cm above sternal angle. S3 gallop present (new finding). No murmurs. Bilateral basal crepitations.
physicalExamination.peripheral: Trace pedal oedema bilaterally. Well-healed sternotomy scar.

investigationResults.ecg: Sinus tachycardia 105. Normal intervals. No ischaemic changes. Voltage slightly reduced from previous.
investigationResults.echocardiogram: LVEF 35% (previous 55%). New global hypokinesis. Mild MR. No pericardial effusion. Normal RV function.
investigationResults.endomyocardialBiopsy: ISHLT Grade 2R (moderate acute cellular rejection). Multifocal infiltrates with myocyte damage. No evidence of antibody-mediated rejection on immunofluorescence.

immediate: IV methylprednisolone 1g daily for 3 days
Increase tacrolimus to 4mg BD targeting level 10-15 ng/mL
Admit for cardiac monitoring and daily observations
Strict fluid balance and daily weights
Frusemide 40mg IV BD for volume overload

medications.name: Methylprednisolone
medications.indication: Pulse steroid therapy for acute rejection

medications.name: Rabbit antithymocyte globulin
medications.frequency: daily x 5 days if no response

investigations: Daily tacrolimus levels until therapeutic
Repeat echo in 1 week to assess response
Repeat endomyocardial biopsy in 2 weeks
DSA (donor-specific antibodies) to exclude AMR
CMV PCR weekly during increased immunosuppression
followUp: Daily transplant team review while inpatient
Medication adherence counselling with transplant pharmacist
Repeat biopsy in 2 weeks to confirm rejection resolution
Weekly clinic visits for 1 month post-discharge
Consider smartphone app for medication reminders

expectedOutcomes: Student recognizes acute cellular rejection presentation
Orders urgent endomyocardial biopsy appropriately
Initiates pulse steroid therapy promptly
Adjusts maintenance immunosuppression based on levels
Addresses medication non-adherence as precipitant

items: Recognizes heart failure signs (S3, elevated JVP) (2 marks)
Links symptoms to possible rejection (1 mark)
Plans repeat biopsy for response assessment (1 mark)
Considers ATG for severe rejection (1 mark)
Counsels on medication adherence importance (1 mark)

commonErrors: Not recognizing subtle rejection symptoms early
Forgetting to check immunosuppression drug levels
Not considering infection as differential diagnosis
Inadequate emphasis on medication adherence
references: ISHLT Guidelines for care of heart transplant recipients (2023)
Transplantation Society of Australia and New Zealand - Post-transplant protocols (2024)
eTG - Organ Transplantation: Cardiac transplant rejection management (2024)

osces.title: Aortic Coarctation - Adult Presentation with Hypertension
osces.scenario: Timothy Walker, a 19-year-old university engineering student, presents to the GP after failing a pre-employment medical due to high blood pressure (165/95 mmHg). He has no symptoms and plays social basketball weekly without limitation. He mentions occasional mild headaches after studying and his calves sometimes ache after running, which he attributed to poor fitness. Family history includes his father having a 'heart murmur' and hypertension diagnosed at age 25. On examination: Well-developed upper body, BP right arm 168/92 mmHg, left arm 164/90 mmHg, HR 72 regular. Cardiovascular examination reveals a late systolic murmur at the left sternal edge and back. Femoral pulses are weak and delayed compared to radial pulses. Lower limb BP (posterior tibial by Doppler) is 110/75 mmHg.
learningObjectives: Recognize clinical features of aortic coarctation in adults
Perform four-limb blood pressure measurement correctly
Identify radio-femoral delay and BP gradient as diagnostic clues
Understand imaging findings including rib notching and figure-3 sign
Plan appropriate surgical vs interventional management
taskInstructions: Take focused cardiovascular history
Perform four-limb blood pressure measurements
Demonstrate radio-femoral delay examination technique
Interpret chest X-ray showing rib notching
Explain CT/MRI findings of coarctation
Discuss management options and long-term complications

patientInformation.name: Timothy Walker
medicalHistory: Mild exercise intolerance attributed to fitness
patientInformation.socialHistory: University student living on campus. Plays social basketball weekly. Non-smoker, occasional alcohol (3-4 beers on weekends). No illicit drugs. Father has hypertension and heart murmur (never investigated). Mother well.

vitalSigns.bloodPressure: Right arm: 168/92 mmHg, Left arm: 164/90 mmHg, Right leg: 112/75 mmHg, Left leg: 110/75 mmHg

physicalExamination.cardiovascular: Prominent carotid pulsations. Late systolic murmur grade 2/6 at left sternal edge, louder over back (interscapular region). Radio-femoral delay present (radial pulse precedes femoral by 60ms). Femoral pulses weak bilaterally. Well-developed upper body musculature, relatively less developed lower limbs.
physicalExamination.peripheral: Prominent collateral vessels visible over back. Posterior tibial and dorsalis pedis pulses palpable but reduced volume.

investigationResults.ecg: Sinus rhythm 72. Left ventricular hypertrophy by voltage criteria (SV1 + RV5 = 42mm). ST-T changes in lateral leads suggesting LV strain.
investigationResults.chestXray: Rib notching of posterior 3rd-8th ribs bilaterally (Roesler sign). Figure-3 sign of aortic knuckle. Mild cardiomegaly. Prominent ascending aorta.
investigationResults.echocardiogram: Coarctation visualized in suprasternal view with turbulent flow. Peak gradient 55 mmHg across coarctation. LVH with wall thickness 13mm. Good LV systolic function. Bicuspid aortic valve with mild regurgitation. Dilated ascending aorta 42mm.
investigationResults.ctAngiography: Severe discrete coarctation just distal to left subclavian artery origin. Minimum diameter 6mm. Extensive collateral circulation via intercostal and internal mammary arteries. Post-stenotic dilatation of descending aorta.

immediate: Start antihypertensive therapy for upper limb hypertension
Avoid strenuous exercise until definitive treatment
Endocarditis prophylaxis counselling (bicuspid valve)
Screen first-degree relatives with echo
Urgent cardiology and cardiac surgery referral
investigations: Cardiac catheterization for hemodynamic assessment
MRI for detailed anatomy and collateral mapping
Exercise stress test for BP response
24-hour ambulatory BP monitoring
Genetic testing for associated syndromes (Turner, Williams-Beuren)
followUp: Cardiac surgery consultation for repair options (end-to-end anastomosis vs subclavian flap vs patch)
Consider balloon angioplasty +/- stenting as alternative
Lifelong cardiac follow-up post-repair (re-coarctation risk)
Annual surveillance for ascending aortic aneurysm
Monitor for persistent hypertension despite repair (35% incidence)

expectedOutcomes: Student performs four-limb BP measurements correctly
Recognizes significant upper-lower limb gradient (>20 mmHg)
Demonstrates radio-femoral delay on examination
Identifies rib notching on chest X-ray
Discusses surgical vs catheter-based interventions appropriately

items: Measures BP in all four limbs correctly (2 marks)
Recognizes coarctation as cause of hypertension (1 mark)
Notes upper-lower limb BP gradient >20 mmHg (1 mark)
Identifies associated bicuspid aortic valve (1 mark)
Identifies rib notching on chest X-ray (1 mark)
Discusses endocarditis risk with bicuspid valve (1 mark)

commonErrors: Not checking BP in all four limbs (missing diagnostic gradient)
Forgetting to examine for radio-femoral delay
Not recognizing rib notching on chest X-ray
Missing associated bicuspid aortic valve
Not screening family members
references: CSANZ Guidelines for management of adult congenital heart disease (2023)
eTG Cardiovascular - Coarctation of the aorta in adults (2024)
ANZSCHS Position statement on adult congenital cardiac surgery (2023)

osces.title: Post-MI Complications - Left Ventricular Free Wall Rupture Recognition
osces.scenario: Maria Stavros, a 68-year-old retired café owner, is day 4 post anterior STEMI treated with delayed PCI (presented 18 hours after symptom onset). She had been recovering well but suddenly develops severe chest pain and dyspnoea at 0600 while getting up to use the bathroom. She appears shocked and distressed. Initial observations: BP 75/50 mmHg (was 125/75 yesterday), HR 125 weak and thready, SpO2 89% on 6L oxygen. JVP elevated to angle of jaw. Heart sounds are muffled. ECG shows sinus tachycardia with low voltage QRS complexes and electrical alternans. Bedside echo shows large pericardial effusion with RV collapse during diastole.
learningObjectives: Recognize acute cardiac tamponade from LV free wall rupture
Understand timing and risk factors for mechanical complications post-MI
Perform emergency pericardiocentesis indications assessment
Coordinate urgent cardiothoracic surgical intervention
Differentiate from other post-MI mechanical complications
taskInstructions: Assess patient with acute deterioration post-MI
Recognize Beck's triad (hypotension, elevated JVP, muffled heart sounds)
Interpret ECG showing electrical alternans
Confirm tamponade physiology on bedside echo
Institute emergency management including pericardiocentesis
Arrange immediate surgical repair

patientInformation.name: Maria Stavros
medicalHistory: Anterior STEMI 4 days ago (delayed presentation - 18 hours)
Primary PCI to LAD with drug-eluting stent
patientInformation.socialHistory: Widowed, lives alone. Two daughters nearby. Retired from running family café 3 years ago. Never smoked. Minimal alcohol. Greek Orthodox faith important to her.

physicalExamination.cardiovascular: JVP to angle of jaw with prominent x-descent, absent y-descent. Heart sounds muffled. No audible murmurs. Pulsus paradoxus 25 mmHg. Peripheral pulses weak.
physicalExamination.respiratory: Tachypnoeic, using accessory muscles. Bibasal crepitations.
physicalExamination.general: Appears shocked, grey, diaphoretic. GCS 14 (E4V4M6 - confused).

investigationResults.ecg: Sinus tachycardia 125. Low voltage QRS (<5mm in limb leads). Electrical alternans (beat-to-beat QRS amplitude variation). Q waves V1-V4 from recent anterior MI.
investigationResults.chestXray: Enlarged cardiac silhouette (water bottle shape). Pulmonary venous congestion. No pneumothorax.
investigationResults.bedsideEcho: Large circumferential pericardial effusion (>30mm). RV collapse in diastole. IVC dilated with no respiratory variation. Swinging heart motion. LV anterior wall akinetic with possible discontinuity near apex.

immediate: CODE BLUE activation - cardiac arrest imminent
Emergency pericardiocentesis - subxiphoid approach with echo guidance
Withhold antiplatelet therapy temporarily
IV fluid resuscitation - 500mL crystalloid stat
Inotropic support - noradrenaline infusion
Prepare for emergency sternotomy and surgical repair
Type and crossmatch 6 units packed red cells
Fresh frozen plasma and platelets available
investigations: Urgent cardiothoracic surgery consultation
Formal echo if time permits for surgical planning
Coagulation profile and thromboelastography
Group and hold, crossmatch blood products
ECG monitoring for arrhythmias
followUp: Emergency surgical repair (patch repair or infarctectomy)
Post-operative ICU care with Swan-Ganz monitoring
IABP or VA-ECMO if required for cardiogenic shock
Gradual reintroduction of antiplatelet therapy post-repair
Long-term heart failure management and rehabilitation

expectedOutcomes: Student recognizes cardiac tamponade presentation urgently
Identifies Beck's triad on examination
Interprets electrical alternans on ECG correctly
Arranges emergency pericardiocentesis
Activates cardiac surgery immediately for definitive repair

items: Identifies electrical alternans on ECG (1 mark)
Notes haemoglobin drop suggesting bleeding (1 mark)
Links presentation to day 3-5 post-MI timing (1 mark)
Differentiates from other mechanical complications (1 mark)
Explains critical situation to patient/family (1 mark)

commonErrors: Delaying pericardiocentesis while awaiting surgical team
Not recognizing electrical alternans as tamponade sign
Giving aggressive diuretics thinking it's just heart failure
Missing pulsus paradoxus on examination
Not stopping antiplatelet therapy before surgery
references: CSANZ Guidelines - Management of acute coronary syndrome complications (2023)
Emergency Medicine Australasia - Cardiac tamponade management protocols (2024)
ANZSCHS Guidelines for emergency cardiac surgery (2023)
